# Night Country

## I. The Other Country

For most of human history, the setting of the sun did not end the day so much as begin another one. Nightfall was not a pause in life but a border crossing — into a place with different laws, different dangers, different possibilities, and a different relationship to the self. Half of everything our species ever experienced, felt, feared, and imagined happened in the dark. We evolved under it. Every ancestor stretching back millions of years fell asleep to sounds instead of screens and woke, sometimes, in the black heart of the night with no lamp to reach for.

Then, in a single century — really in a handful of generations — we did something unprecedented in the history of life on Earth: we abolished the night. We pushed it back behind curtains and beyond city limits, thinned it into a brief inconvenience between one lit room and the next. It may be worth asking what the night actually was, all those thousands of years, before we decided it was merely the absence of something better. Because the answer turns out to be stranger than darkness. The answer involves a lost way of sleeping, a vanished hour of the soul, and a river of light that a third of humanity has never seen.

## II. First Sleep and Second

In the 1980s and 90s, the historian Roger Ekirch began noticing something peculiar in the archives of early modern Europe. Again and again, in court records, letters, diaries, medical treatises, and works of literature, he encountered the phrase "first sleep." It was not being used poetically. Chaucer refers to it plainly. Italian documents speak of the *primo sonno*. Sixteenth-century physicians advising couples who wished to conceive recommended the effort be made after the first sleep — implying, matter-of-factly, that everyone knew what the first sleep was and when it ended.

The picture that emerges from thousands of these references is striking: for centuries, Westerners did not sleep through the night. They went to bed shortly after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours — what some sources called the "dead sleep" — and then woke, quite naturally, around midnight. They stayed awake for an hour or more, and then returned to bed for a "second sleep" that lasted until dawn. This was not insomnia and it was not eccentricity. It was, as far as anyone can tell, the default architecture of human sleep.

That midnight interval had a life of its own. Devotional writers treasured it as the purest hour for prayer, when the mind was uncluttered by the day's noise — a conviction built into monastic vigils long before. Families tended the fire, smoked, talked. Neighbors visited neighbors. Lovers took advantage of the privacy. Court records note thefts committed in the quiet of the watch, which is what the interval was sometimes simply called. Washington Irving, writing in the 1820s, looked back on the old custom with something like grief, observing that his contemporaries now slept straight through what their grandparents had experienced — an hour of wakefulness in the middle of the night that seemed, in his telling, to produce thoughts unlike anything the daylight hours could offer.

Here is the part that makes the story more than a curiosity. In the 1990s, the psychiatrist Thomas Wehr ran an experiment at the National Institutes of Mental Health in which volunteers were given fourteen hours of darkness every day — mimicking a natural winter photoperiod — for a month. After a period of paying off accumulated sleep debt, the subjects settled into a striking pattern: their sleep split cleanly into two episodes, separated by a stretch of calm wakefulness lasting an hour or two. During that interlude, their brains hummed with elevated prolactin, and the subjects described the state as something close to meditation — serene, alert, unlike ordinary waking consciousness. Given enough darkness, the two-sleep pattern re-emerged on its own, as though it had been waiting inside us all along.

If Wehr and Ekirch are right, then a familiar modern affliction deserves a reinterpretation. Waking at three in the morning with a restless, wandering mind may not be a malfunction. It may be a fossil — the ancient watch surfacing through our expectations — and much of the suffering comes not from the waking itself but from the alarm at finding ourselves awake, in a lit room, checking a glowing phone, convinced that sleep is supposed to arrive in one unbroken eight-hour slab. Perhaps some wakefulness has always belonged to the night.

## III. The Economics of Darkness

Why did people simply accept the dark? Partly because light cost money — real money, budgeted like bread. Tallow candles smoked and stank and had to be earned; beeswax burned sweetly but belonged mostly to churches and the wealthy. The poor made do with rushlights — dried rushes dipped in kitchen grease — that gave off a feeble, guttering glow for a fraction of the price. A laborer reckoning the week's expenses counted candles alongside flour. Darkness was not a preference; it was an economy.

Law reinforced economy. The very word *curfew* descends from the Old French *couvre-feu* — "cover the fire" — the signal that hearths should be banked and streets abandoned. William the Conqueror rang such bells across England. Medieval statutes required towns to keep their gates, clear their streets, and post watches; to be abroad at night without reason was to invite arrest as a "nightwalker." Courts treated darkness almost as an accomplice, an aggravating circumstance written into the character of a crime. Night, legally speaking, was foreign territory.

And physically, it was genuinely perilous. Unlit streets were mazes of open cellar doors, unstable paving, and worse. Those who ventured out hired linkboys carrying flaming torches, or carried lanterns themselves; Samuel Pepys records the ritual anxieties of walking home through London after dark. Night labor existed — bakers, printers, the men who collected the city's waste before dawn — but it was the exception, and it was punishing. For nearly everyone else, the sun's departure meant the practical end of activity, and bedtime was early, communal, and non-negotiable.

## IV. Terror and Liberty

Yet the same darkness that frightened people also freed them, and any honest portrait of the old night has to hold both faces at once.

The terror was real and culturally enormous. Night was when the dead walked, when revenants knocked at doors, when the thing that gave the *nightmare* its name — the *mare*, a demon believed to sit upon sleepers' chests — went about its work. Stripped of sight, the mind did not go quiet; it manufactured. Every creak became a footstep, every shadow an intruder, because imagination unchecked by evidence filled vacuums fast. The stories families told by firelight — ghost stories, fairy tales, tales of the road — were calibrated for exactly this state: the teller, the listeners, the dark pressing at the edge of the flame. Oral tradition had its native habitat, and it was night.

But night was also the one great commons that the powerful could not fully fence. Servants gossiped after their masters slept. Apprentices slipped out to taverns. Smugglers and poachers ran entire parallel economies by the light of the moon. Lovers met. And for enslaved people in the Americas, the dark was cover for escape and for forbidden gatherings of worship; the song of the Drinking Gourd turned the Big Dipper into a compass pointed north, whatever the exact historical reach of its use. The night belonged, in practice, to those whose days belonged to someone else. It was the poor's own country.

## V. The River of Light

Above all of this hung the sky. For every generation before the last few, the greatest spectacle available anywhere on Earth — free, nightly, inexhaustible — was overhead. The Milky Way did not require imagination to see. It arched from horizon to horizon, a luminous river, and nearly every culture that ever lived built mythology along its banks.

It was infrastructure, too. Sailors steered by the pole star; Pacific navigators held entire star-path charts in memory, reading swells and stars together across thousands of miles of open ocean. Farmers kept calendars by the Pleiades, whose seasonal risings announced planting time to Greeks, to Māori celebrating the new year at Matariki, to Japanese observers who gave that cluster a name — Subaru — now driving around on the back of every hatchback.

And here is a detail worth savoring: some cultures found their constellations not in the stars but in the dark. Aboriginal Australian astronomers read the shadowy dust lanes of the Milky Way and saw the Emu in the Sky, a great bird traced in darkness itself. Andean peoples likewise picked out figures in the black patches — a celestial llama among them. Darkness, in other words, was legible. It was meaningful, inhabited, part of the text. The night sky was humanity's shared broadcast, playing for a hundred thousand years to an audience of everyone, and each generation added its layer of story to the last.

## VI. Putting Out the Stars

The dismantling happened in stages. Gaslight arrived first, in the early nineteenth century, and London and Paris began to glow — Paris earning its title as the City of Light. Gas extended commerce and policing deep into the hours that had previously belonged to sleep, and the night shift was born. Then, in 1882, Edison's Pearl Street station began sending electricity into lower Manhattan, and within a few decades the night became, for the first time in the history of the planet, optional.

The scale of what followed is hard to absorb. According to the landmark 2016 world atlas of artificial night brightness, more than eighty percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies, and the Milky Way is hidden from fully a third of our species — including sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans. Skyglow travels hundreds of kilometers from its sources. Each generation grows up with a dimmer baseline and assumes that dimness is normal.

As the story goes, on January 17, 1994, the Northridge earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, and the Griffith Observatory received calls from residents alarmed by an immense, strange, silvery cloud that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. Some callers, living their whole lives under urban light, had never seen it except as a rumor.

The costs radiate outward. Sea turtle hatchlings instinctively scramble toward the brighter horizon — which, for a hundred million years, meant the moonlit sea — and now they crawl inland toward parking lots and die by the thousands upon thousands each season. In the United States alone, hundreds of millions of birds a year perish in building collisions, many of them pulled off course by illuminated towers, which is why cities now dim their skylines during migration in "Lights Out" campaigns. Insects spiral to their deaths around porch lights; pollinators lose their bearings; even trees near streetlights bud out of season. And we are not exempt: blue-rich light suppresses melatonin, scrambles circadian rhythms, and is increasingly implicated in the modern epidemic of bad sleep — the epidemic that sends so many of us, ironically, to lie awake at 3 a.m., staring at ceilings that never get truly dark.

## VII. Keeping the Dark

None of this is a call for nostalgia, and honesty requires saying so. Artificial light has been a magnificent liberation. It ended the constant fire hazard of open flames, made streets walkable, let ordinary people read and study after a day's labor, brought the sick competent care at 3 a.m., and dissolved the genuine terrors that made the dark a tyranny for the vulnerable. Light, like every powerful technology, gave with one hand and took with the other. The question was never whether to take the gift. The question is whether we can learn to ration it — whether we can treat darkness the way we have slowly learned to treat wild rivers and old forests: not as wasted space awaiting improvement, but as something scarce, valuable, and worth protecting on purpose.

Encouragingly, the project has begun. DarkSky International certifies places that defend their night skies; Flagstaff, Arizona, home of a great observatory, became the first Dark Sky City in 2001 and remains safely, adequately lit — just intelligently, with shielded fixtures and warm tones aimed down instead of scattered up. More cities join the migration-season blackouts every year. On the personal scale, the entry price is almost embarrassingly low: go outside on a clear, moonless night, get away from the worst glare if you can, and wait. Full dark adaptation takes half an hour, and it is one of the strangest experiences left to us — the sky swelling into a dome with depth, the faint band resolving, thousands of stars arriving that were technically present all along, waiting behind the veil of your own impatience.

But perhaps the deeper recovery is temporal rather than scenic: the return of the watch. It is suggestive that so many traditions, independently, built sacred practice around the small hours — monastic vigils, the Islamic tahajjud, the Jewish tikkun chatzot at midnight, the Hindu brahma muhurta before dawn. All of them intuited what Wehr's subjects rediscovered in a laboratory: that certain hours yield a quality of mind unavailable in daylight, a calm, drifting, half-dreaming attentiveness in which thoughts surface that the busy brain normally drowns out. Writers have always raided this borderland for material; insomniacs have always suffered in it unnecessarily. If you wake at 3 a.m. sometimes, consider that you may not be broken. You may simply be standing in a very old doorway.

Go out, sometime soon, and look up. Behind the orange haze, patient as ever, the same river of light that our ancestors steered by and named and prayed beneath still crosses the heavens, undiminished, indifferent to whether anyone attends. The dark was never empty. It is the condition under which everything else becomes visible — the rest of the galaxy, and the quieter registers of our own minds, the ones that only speak when the lights go out. We spent a hundred thousand years learning what the night could give us, and fifty years throwing it away. Keep a little of it. Keep it the way we keep wilderness: not because we mean to live there, but because something ancient in us still knows the way home.
